newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS - BHP hopes for copper price rise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BHP hopes for copper price rise.

text.p: The world's number two copper producer and Australia's largest listed company, The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd, said on Friday it hoped -- but would not predict -- world copper prices would hold up this year.

"The fundamentals of the industry we think are a little stronger than we were assessing them to be six or nine months ago and we are hoping rather than predicting that the strength that we've seen in recent weeks will continue at least into the next calendar year," BHP managing director John Prescott told reporters.
The company reported earlier on Friday that net profit in the year to May 31 fell by 60.8 percent to A$410 million after abnormal items of A$976 million.
More than half of the abnormal loss, A$550 million, was due to write-downs at the recently-acquired North American copper operation.

In a surprise disclosure Prescott said the North American copper operations did not form part of the group's "key core businesses," despite BHP having paid US$2.4 billion for Arizona-based Magma Copper Co in 1996.

Prescott said a comprehensive review of assets had concluded that core busineses were limited to the offshore Bass Strait oil and gas fields, the offshore North-West Shelf liquefied natural gas project, parts of the steel business, the Escondida copper mine in Chile, iron ore and "strong parts of the coal business".
All other operating assets were classed below these in a category where asset sales would be considered.
A further three categories held projects under development but not yet commissioned, others awaiting the go-ahead and "incubator" projects which are in their very early stages.
One bright spot in the copper business was an expectation of a rise in measured copper reserves at the Magma operations.
"There will be a build up in the reserves," Prescott said.

He also stressed some positives in the Magma operation that had yet to be reflected in BHP's accounts, referring to the expected increase in reserves. But the executive failed to quantify the expected increase.
Sales revenue from the copper division for the year was A$3.8 billion, 28 percent above last year,

The increase was due to inclusion of the Magma operations and increased shipments from the Escondida mine in Chile, only partly offset by lower Ok Tedi shipments from Papua New Guinea and lower average copper prices.
Copper prices, which were depressed for most of the first half of the year, partially recovered in the past six months, the company noted.
The average price BHP booked for copper shipments in the year was US$1.06 a pound versus US$1.18 the previous year.
Unhedged copper shipments not finalised as of May 31 have been brought to account at US$1.10 per pound.
The London Metal Exchange copper spot price at 30 May 1997 was US$1.18 per pound, against US$1.15 per pound at 31 May 1996.
For the year to May 31, 1998, 16 percent of projected copper sales are covered by put options at an average price of US$0.89 a pound, BHP said.
For the same period, 16 percent of projected copper sales are covered by forward contracts at an average price of US$1.01 a pound, it said.
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
